pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 1 of the Long Walk. Weather: fair. Distance: three miles. Direction: (an ink blot).*

Most mornings on the mountain began with a bell, and this one did too, though it was the wrong sort of bell: a single cracked clang from the rope tower, the kind you ring when a goat has got into the cheese.

Highstep was a village of two hundred and twelve people, forty goats, one bell tower and a great many ropes, and it sat among the pines on the shoulders of a mountain called Tor. This is not the usual arrangement for a village. But then Tor was not the usual sort of mountain. She had four legs, each the size of a hill. She had a long low head with two grey stone horns, and a back so thickly furred with moss and pine that you could live on it for years without noticing she breathed. And every spring, for as long as anyone had kept a Walk-Book, she had woken up and walked the same great circle of the land, three miles a day, with the whole of Highstep riding along and complaining about the bumps.
pages.image: A vast gentle mountain-sized creature named Tor walks across a green spring landscape at sunrise; her broad mossy back is covered in pine forest with a small hillside village of tiny cottages, a rope tower and rope bridges perched on her shoulders, her long low head with two grey stone horns and kind small eyes lifted toward the light.

pages.text:
Mo Ferreira did not need the bell. Mo was already awake, because Mo was always awake for the first step of the Long Walk. He stood on the flat stone of the Footpost in the middle of the village, barefoot, with his eyes shut and his toes spread, waiting for the whole of Highstep to lean the way it had leaned every spring of his life.

He was eleven, small and wiry, in a patched green poncho with a rope belt and a brass plumb-bob that knocked against his knee. He was never seen in shoes. When people asked why not, he said shoes were like wearing mittens to read.

Because Mo could feel Tor. Everyone in Highstep felt her walk, the way you feel a cart on a bad road, but Mo felt more. Through the soles of his feet he could tell when she was sleepy, or pleased, or itching where a squirrel had settled. It was called the Footsense. His Gran said there had been one in every other generation for eleven hundred years, and that it was a great gift, and that it did not excuse him from washing.

Under his heels, this morning, the mountain was waking. He felt the slow roll of her great shoulders. He felt a deep, warm hum in his teeth.
pages.image: Mo, a small wiry 11-year-old boy with warm brown skin, untidy black hair, bare dusty feet, a patched green poncho and a rope belt with a brass plumb-bob, stands with eyes closed and toes spread on a flat round stone in the middle of a hilltop village of small timber houses, a quiet smile on his face as morning light comes through the pines.

pages.text:
"She's awake," said Junie Achebe, arriving in a hurry with a hammer in her belt, which was normal, and a piece of Mo's washing in her teeth, which was not.

"That's mine," said Mo, without opening his eyes.

"It was on the goat."

Junie was eleven, too, and tall, with a great round puff of dark curls tied up in a yellow scarf, and a leather tool-belt so full of nails and pegs that it clinked when she walked. She was Mo's best friend, which meant she was allowed to be rude to him before breakfast. She fixed things. It was a family habit: her father built houses and her mother wove them curtains, and in all of Highstep there was nobody who could tell you as quickly what was crooked.

"My floor's tipped again," she said, handing over the sock. "Three degrees. I measured. One day," she said, and here she looked at the stone, and then away, "I'm going to live in a house that doesn't lean."

"It leans because we walk," said Mo.

"I know why it leans," said Junie. "That's not the same as liking it."

Behind them, Admiral the goat, who was huge, brown and white and owned one crooked horn and a tin bell, ate the rest of somebody's shirt.
pages.image: Junie, a tall 11-year-old with dark brown skin, a big round puff of black curls tied up in a yellow scarf and a leather tool-belt full of nails and pegs, hands a rumpled sock to Mo, who stands barefoot in a green poncho, while Admiral, a huge brown and white goat with one crooked horn and a tin bell, chews a shirt beside them on the village green.

pages.text:
The village got ready as it did every spring. On the rope tower, Mo's father Tomás, who was large and gentle and mended the ropes that held Highstep up, checked knots and whistled through his teeth. Down in the cheese caves Mo's mother Marisol was carrying wheels of cheese as big as cartwheels down to the cellar, three at a time, with a look on her face that said she would be glad if nobody spoke to her. Mayor Marsh, round and brisk in a tall hat with a green sash, hurried across the Green with a clipboard, ringing the Starting Bell and reminding people that a village is only as orderly as its lists.

And in the middle of it all, at her tall desk by the Footpost, sat Mo's Gran, the Stepkeeper. Ada Ferreira was tiny and upright, with a white braid to her waist, spectacles as big as saucers and a walking staff with a small brass bell on top. She kept the Walk-Book, which was the story of every day Highstep had ever walked. She wrote it down in ink. She had a thumb permanently stained blue.

"Weather," she said, licking her pen. "Fair. Distance, three miles, as ever. Mo, are you ready?"

"I'm always ready," said Mo.

"That," said Gran, "is exactly what worries me."
pages.image: A busy morning on a hilltop village green: Mo's father Tomás, a large gentle man with coils of rope over his shoulder, on a wooden rope tower; Mayor Marsh, a round woman in a tall hat with a green sash, holding a clipboard; and Gran, a tiny upright old woman with a long white braid, huge round spectacles and a tall staff with a small brass bell, writing in a big book at a desk.

pages.text:
Tor took her first step.

It was a good step, a big slow ordinary step that rolled through the whole village like a wave through a bathtub. The goats leaned. The washing swung. Somebody's teacup slid gently to the end of its table, as it did every year, and was caught by somebody else, as it did every year.

Then Tor took her second step, and Mo's eyes flew open.

It had come down a little to the left.

He knew it before anyone. He knew it in his heels. The Old Road ran to the right, through the birch gap, down toward the Spring Meadows, and it always had. He looked; there was the gap in the trees, pale and green and expecting them. And the mountain, calmly, unhurriedly, was not going to it.

By the third step everybody could feel it. A wheel of cheese rolled off a table. The Starting Bell clanged by itself. The Mayor's hat slid over one eye. On the Footpost, Gran, with her pen still in the air, went completely still, and where the word for the direction should have gone, a single drop of ink fell and spread.

Ahead of Highstep, for the first time in a thousand years, lay a road that nobody had ever walked.
pages.image: Tor, a colossal moss-backed mountain-creature with a village on her shoulders, has just turned left off a green valley road, leaving a pale gap between birch trees behind her; on the village green tiny villagers stumble, a cheese wheel rolls, Mayor Marsh's tall hat slips over one eye, and Mo stares wide-eyed while old Gran holds her pen still above a big book with a single blot of ink.
